Fix a four-dimensional smooth spacetime region $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with a stated orientation, spin structure, boundary conditions, and unit system. A selected model specifies a continuous global symmetry group $H$, its action on the fields and observables, the nondynamical background connections, the field and jet domains, a regulator and measure or formal perturbative generating functional, and the admissible local counterterms. A background connection is nondynamical model data: it transforms under local changes of background trivialization but is not integrated over.

Let $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{bg},U}^{g,p}$ be the finite-jet horizontal $p$-forms of ghost number $g$ generated by the nondynamical background connections and their BRST ghost jets, without matter-field jets. Fix their coefficient field $\mathbb K$ as part of the model and restrict its nilpotent BRST differential $s$ and horizontal exterior derivative $d_H$ to this background subalgebra, with $s^2=d_H^2=sd_H+d_Hs=0$. The model supplies two $\mathbb K$-linear subspaces

$$\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal A_{\mathrm{bg},U}^{0,4},\qquad\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal A_{\mathrm{bg},U}^{1,3}.$$

Here $\mathcal C$ is exactly the space of admissible changes of local background counterterm density, with coefficients and units giving dimensionless integrated action changes. The space $\mathcal N$ is exactly the space of boundary primitives whose $d_H$-derivatives are discarded in the infinitesimal variation under the stated support or boundary conditions. This convention must hold on every admitted background and ghost input; a surface contribution that is not discarded is not an element of $d_H\mathcal N$. Linearity of these two spaces is explicit model input, not a consequence of locality or nilpotence. No linear span of a restricted admissibility set is taken implicitly. If quantization or other restrictions instead make the admissible changes nonlinear, this vector-space quotient does not apply to them without a separately specified equivalence structure.

The space of compatible Wess–Zumino cocycles and the space of admissible changes are

$$Z^{1,4}:=\{a\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{bg},U}^{1,4}:sa+d_Hb=0\text{ for some }b\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{bg},U}^{2,3}\},\qquad B_{\mathcal C,\mathcal N}:=s\mathcal C+d_H\mathcal N.$$

Both are linear spaces, and $B_{\mathcal C,\mathcal N}\subseteq Z^{1,4}$: for $a=sc+d_Hn$ choose the ghost-number-two three-form $b=sn$, giving $sa+d_Hb=s^2c+sd_Hn+d_Hsn=0$. More generally, if $sa+d_Hb=0$, then $a'=a+sc+d_Hn$ obeys $sa'+d_H(b+sn)=0$, so every admitted representative change preserves consistency. The witness space for $b$ has bidegree $(2,3)$ and is distinct from the boundary-ambiguity space $\mathcal N$ of bidegree $(1,3)$.

An infinitesimal local anomaly representative is a specified $a_4\in Z^{1,4}$ for the model's quantum background variation. The **local perturbative ’t Hooft anomaly** is its class in

$$H^{1,4}_{\mathcal C,\mathcal N}(s\mid d_H):=Z^{1,4}/B_{\mathcal C,\mathcal N},\qquad a'_4\sim a_4\ \Longleftrightarrow\ a'_4-a_4=sc+d_Hn\text{ for some }c\in\mathcal C,\ n\in\mathcal N.$$

The subspace property makes this an equivalence relation and a quotient vector space. Its class is zero exactly when $a_4=sc+d_Hn$ for some such $c,n$; adding the admissible counterterm density $-c$ then leaves only the discarded term $d_Hn$. Conversely, if adding an admissible density $c'$ leaves a discarded term, $a_4+sc'=d_Hn$, then $a_4=s(-c')+d_Hn$ has zero class. This is precisely cancellation of the infinitesimal local background variation in the declared convention. The ordinary unrestricted relative cohomology $H^{1,4}(s\mid d_H)$ is the special case $\mathcal C=\mathcal A_{\mathrm{bg},U}^{0,4}$ and $\mathcal N=\mathcal A_{\mathrm{bg},U}^{1,3}$ with a boundary convention discarding all these total derivatives; it is not substituted for a restricted model quotient.

Any prescribed noninvariance of the classical action or selected couplings is an explicit-symmetry-breaking insertion and is separated before assigning this quantum anomaly class. It is not, by itself, a measure anomaly. A claim of anomaly matching therefore assumes the stated classical symmetry, or carries such breaking insertions separately.

This definition applies to a global symmetry whose background is nondynamical. If the same local class concerns a field integrated over as a gauge redundancy, it is a local gauge anomaly, not a ’t Hooft anomaly; an uncancelled gauge anomaly obstructs the proposed gauging unless a separately specified cancellation mechanism is included. The definition addresses only infinitesimal transformations and makes no claim about large or disconnected transformations, determinant-line holonomy, torsion phases, or a physical continuum limit.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold, $G$ a finite-dimensional real Lie group, $\pi:P\to M$ a smooth right principal $G$-bundle, and $\omega$ the principal connection 1-form of a supplied horizontal distribution. Fix a finite-dimensional complex representation $\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ that is smooth, and let $E=P\times_\rho V$ be its associated vector bundle with relation $[pg,v]=[p,\rho(g)v]$. Define $\rho_*:=d\rho_e:\mathfrak g\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, where the differential is taken after viewing $\rho$ as a smooth matrix-valued map. For any open cover with smooth local sections $s_i:U_i\to P$, write $A_i=s_i^*\omega$. A smooth section $\sigma$ of $E$ has unique local components $\psi_i:U_i\to V$ given by $\sigma(x)=[s_i(x),\psi_i(x)]$. Define the **associated covariant derivative** $\nabla^\omega\sigma$ by its local components

$$
(\nabla^\omega\sigma)_i=d\psi_i+\rho_*(A_i)\psi_i,
$$

where $(\rho_*(A_i)\psi_i)(X)=\rho_*(A_i(X))\psi_i$ for $X\in TU_i$. These expressions patch to a smooth $E$-valued 1-form on $M$, independently of the chosen local sections, and satisfy $\nabla^\omega(f\sigma)=df\otimes\sigma+f\nabla^\omega\sigma$ for every smooth scalar function $f$ on $M$.

Let V→X be an oriented Euclidean real vector bundle of rank n, with oriented frame bundle P_SO(V). Use Spin(n)=Spin_N=1(ℝⁿ,−‖·‖²), the norm-one even subgroup of the negative-square Clifford algebra, and its standard twisted-Clifford homomorphism λ_n:Spin(n)→SO(n). A Spin structure on V is a principal Spin(n)-bundle P with a Spin(n)-equivariant two-fold map $\widetilde\lambda:P\to P_{SO}(V)$ covering the identity on X and satisfying $\widetilde\lambda(pg)=\widetilde\lambda(p)\lambda_n(g)$. Put $\operatorname{Spin}^c(n)=(\operatorname{Spin}(n)\times U(1))/\langle(-1,-1)\rangle$ and define $\lambda_n^c:\operatorname{Spin}^c(n)\to SO(n)$ by $\lambda_n^c([s,z])=\lambda_n(s)$. A Spin$^c$ structure is a principal Spin$^c(n)$-bundle $P_c$ with a $\operatorname{Spin}^c(n)$-equivariant map $\widetilde\lambda_c:P_c\to P_{SO}(V)$ over the identity satisfying $\widetilde\lambda_c(p g)=\widetilde\lambda_c(p)\lambda_n^c(g)$. A spinor bundle is the associated bundle for the specified real Clifford representation; a Spin$^c$ spinor bundle is $P_c\times_{\tau^c}S$, where the specified complex representation $\tau$ of $\operatorname{Spin}(n)$ and integer $U(1)$ weight $k$ satisfy $\tau(-1)(-1)^k=I_S$, and $\tau^c([s,z])=z^k\tau(s)$. This condition is exactly that $(-1,-1)$ act trivially, so the representation descends to the quotient. For the complex Clifford spinor representation, $\tau(-1)=-I_S$ and the standard weight is $k=1$. These are given structures; this definition asserts no existence criterion.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb F$
([[def-banach-space]]) and let $T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is a **Fredholm operator** when
all three of the following hold:

1. $\ker T$ is finite dimensional, that is, admits an ordered basis of finite
   length ([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-dimension]]);
2. $\operatorname{ran}T$ is a closed subspace of $Y$
   ([[def-linear-subspace]]);
3. the **cokernel** $\operatorname{coker}T:=Y/\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite
   dimensional ([[def-quotient-vector-space-coset-notation]],
   [[def-dimension]]).

Here the cokernel is the algebraic quotient vector space; it also carries the
quotient seminorm of [[def-quotient-seminorm]], which is a norm when the range
is closed ([[thm-quotient-seminorm-is-a-norm-iff-subspace-is-closed]]), but the dimension in clause 3 is the vector-space dimension of the
quotient and does not depend on that norm.

For a Fredholm operator $T$ the **index** of $T$ is the integer

$$\operatorname{ind}T:=\dim_{\mathbb F}\ker T-\dim_{\mathbb F}\operatorname{coker}T$$

Here subtraction is in $\mathbb Z$, not in $\mathbb N$: write $a=\dim_{\mathbb F}\ker T$ and $b=\dim_{\mathbb F}\operatorname{coker}T$ and identify a natural $n$ with $[(n,0)]$. Precisely,

$$\operatorname{ind}T=[(a,b)]=[(a,0)]+(-[(b,0)])\in\mathbb Z$$

by [[def-integers]] and [[def-int-operations]]. Both dimensions are natural numbers, so this class is defined even when $a<b$; the index may be positive, negative or zero.

**Two remarks on the definition.** The closedness of the range is listed
explicitly as a hypothesis of the definition rather than extracted from the
other clauses. And no property of the index is asserted here; additivity,
local constancy and invariance under compact perturbations are separate
theorems.

derivations.claim: By [A1], each kernel and cokernel is finite-dimensional, so each top exterior power in the Definition is a one-dimensional complex vector space. The explicit invertible-band transitions supply the smooth line even across kernel jumps; the stated spectral identities give the cut-independent Quillen norm, and [A1] supplies the smooth compatible connection. Their tensor product and dual are therefore a one-dimensional Hermitian line with the specified Quillen metric.

Gauge covariance of the Dirac operators intertwines kernel and cokernel unitarily, and the conjugate operators have the same spectrum, so the endpoint map preserves the specified Quillen metric. Parallel transport is unitary. Therefore $u_*^{-1}\circ\mathrm{PT}_{A_t}$ is a unitary automorphism of a one-dimensional complex line, hence multiplication by a unique scalar of modulus one. A change of unit vector in the fiber conjugates that scalar, which does not change it because $U(1)$ is abelian. Therefore $\operatorname{Hol}_{\gamma}(\mathcal L)$ is a well-defined element of $U(1)$. By [F1], the local anomaly interface does not classify determinant-line holonomy; this phase is defined here as separate global loop data, not as a consequence of [F1].

$$D^+_{A,R}:H^1(M;S^+\otimes E_R)\longrightarrow L^2(M;S^-\otimes E_R),\qquad D^+_{A,R}\psi=\sum_{i=1}^{d} c(e_i)\nabla_{e_i}\psi\quad(\psi\in C^\infty(M;S^+\otimes E_R)),$$

$$\mathcal L_A=\left(\det_{\mathbb C}\ker D^+_{A,R}\right)^*\otimes\det_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{coker}D^+_{A,R},$$

Here $\det_{\mathbb C}W=\bigwedge^{\dim_{\mathbb C}W}_{\mathbb C}W$, including $\det0=\mathbb C$. Our phrase **inverse determinant line** means the dual of $\Delta_A=\det\ker D^+\otimes(\det\operatorname{coker}D^+)^*$; the displayed $\mathcal L$ is the line called $\mathrm{Det}$, not $\mathrm{Det}^{-1}$, in Dai–Freed §2. This explicit formula fixes the convention throughout.

The named regularized geometry means the following supplied **admissible analytic data**, rather than an arbitrary Hermitian line relabeled by a name. Test smooth dependence on each finite-dimensional smooth parameter manifold $T$ of connections on the fixed $M,P,R$. Write $\mathscr H^\pm=T\times L^2(M;S^\pm\otimes E_R)$ with common first-Sobolev domains. Supply unitary parameter connections $\widetilde\nabla^\pm$ on these Hilbert bundles, preserving smooth sections and the Sobolev domains; for the fixed product identification one may take the ordinary derivative in $T$. Fix a positive inverse-length scale $\mu$ and put $\mathscr D=D^+/\mu$, with Hilbert adjoint $\mathscr D^*$. These choices and the local-counterterm convention are fixed before phases are compared.

Require $Q^+=\mathscr D^*\mathscr D$ and $Q^-=\mathscr D\mathscr D^*$ to have the supplied nonnegative self-adjoint realizations with discrete spectrum, finite multiplicities and smooth eigensections, and the same positive spectrum with multiplicity. A spectral cut is a number $a>0$ not in either spectrum on an open parameter patch $U_a\subseteq T$. Gauge identifications must intertwine all cut data, preserve this norm and preserve the connection after the corresponding parameter pullback. Parallel transport means the solution of $\nabla^{\mathrm{BF}}_{\dot A_t}s(t)=0$ with a specified initial value; in a unit frame with connection $i\beta$, it is multiplication by $\exp(-i\int\beta)$.

When the supplied real or pseudoreal fermion structure instead yields a skew-Fredholm quadratic form, include its actual **Pfaffian data**. For a finite $2m$-dimensional space $W$ the Pfaffian is $\operatorname{pf}(b)=b^{\wedge m}/m!\in\det W^*$, interpreting $b\in\bigwedge^2W^*$; it is zero in odd dimension. Glue $P_a=\det W_a^*$ by the nonzero Pfaffians of the even-dimensional invertible cut bands. The resulting graded line $P$ has parity $\dim\ker B\bmod2$ and the specified natural square identification $P^{\otimes2}\cong L_B$, where $L_B$ is the displayed determinant convention applied to $B$. Its squared Quillen norm has high-mode factor $\exp(-\zeta'_{B,a}(0)/2)$, with $\zeta_{B,a}$ defined from $B^*B$ exactly as above. Its unitary connection is the one whose tensor square, under that identification, is the supplied Bismut–Freed connection of $L_B$; locally its connection form is half that determinant form in square-compatible frames. Smooth gluing, the square identification, spectral continuations, metric compatibility and gauge naturality are required Pfaffian admissibility data, not an arbitrary choice of a square root or an existence assertion for every real/pseudoreal theory.

This definition applies to a global symmetry whose background is nondynamical. If the same local class concerns a field integrated over as a gauge redundancy, it is a local gauge anomaly, not a ’t Hooft anomaly; an uncancelled gauge anomaly obstructs the proposed gauging unless a separately specified cancellation mechanism is included. The definition addresses only infinitesimal transformations and makes no claim about large or disconnected transformations, determinant-line holonomy, torsion phases, or a physical continuum limit.

Let V→X be an oriented Euclidean real vector bundle of rank n, with oriented frame bundle P_SO(V). Use Spin(n)=Spin_N=1(ℝⁿ,−‖·‖²), the norm-one even subgroup of the negative-square Clifford algebra, and its standard twisted-Clifford homomorphism λ_n:Spin(n)→SO(n). A Spin structure on V is a principal Spin(n)-bundle P with a Spin(n)-equivariant two-fold map $\widetilde\lambda:P\to P_{SO}(V)$ covering the identity on X and satisfying $\widetilde\lambda(pg)=\widetilde\lambda(p)\lambda_n(g)$. Put $\operatorname{Spin}^c(n)=(\operatorname{Spin}(n)\times U(1))/\langle(-1,-1)\rangle$ and define $\lambda_n^c:\operatorname{Spin}^c(n)\to SO(n)$ by $\lambda_n^c([s,z])=\lambda_n(s)$. A Spin$^c$ structure is a principal Spin$^c(n)$-bundle $P_c$ with a $\operatorname{Spin}^c(n)$-equivariant map $\widetilde\lambda_c:P_c\to P_{SO}(V)$ over the identity satisfying $\widetilde\lambda_c(p g)=\widetilde\lambda_c(p)\lambda_n^c(g)$. A spinor bundle is the associated bundle for the specified real Clifford representation; a Spin$^c$ spinor bundle is $P_c\times_{\tau^c}S$, where the specified complex representation $\tau$ of $\operatorname{Spin}(n)$ and integer $U(1)$ weight $k$ satisfy $\tau(-1)(-1)^k=I_S$, and $\tau^c([s,z])=z^k\tau(s)$. This condition is exactly that $(-1,-1)$ act trivially, so the representation descends to the quotient. For the complex Clifford spinor representation, $\tau(-1)=-I_S$ and the standard weight is $k=1$. These are given structures; this definition asserts no existence criterion.

Equip $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ with its finite-dimensional real topology, Pin and full-even Spin with the subspace topology, and $O(V,B)$ and $SO(V,B)$ with their matrix topologies. The maps in [[thm-real-pin-spin-image-kernel-and-compactness]] are continuous central two-sheeted covering maps. This is a topological assertion in addition to the algebraic exactness of those sequences.

Let
$(\mathcal C,\otimes,\mathbf 1,\alpha,\lambda,\rho)$ and
$(\mathcal D,\boxtimes,\mathbf 1',\alpha',\lambda',\rho')$
be monoidal categories ([[def-monoidal-category]]).

A **lax monoidal functor** is a functor
$F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ ([[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]])
together with natural transformations ([[def-natural-transformation]])

$$F_{2;X,Y}:F(X)\boxtimes F(Y)\longrightarrow F(X\otimes Y),$$

and

the morphism

$$F_0:\mathbf 1'\longrightarrow F(\mathbf 1),$$

such that, for all $X,Y,Z$,

$$F(\alpha_{X,Y,Z})\circ F_{2;X\otimes Y,Z}\circ(F_{2;X,Y}\boxtimes1_{F(Z)})=F_{2;X,Y\otimes Z}\circ(1_{F(X)}\boxtimes F_{2;Y,Z})\circ\alpha'_{F(X),F(Y),F(Z)},$$

$$F(\lambda_X)\circ F_{2;\mathbf 1,X}\circ(F_0\boxtimes1_{F(X)})=\lambda'_{F(X)},$$

$$F(\rho_X)\circ F_{2;X,\mathbf 1}\circ(1_{F(X)}\boxtimes F_0)=\rho'_{F(X)}.$$

A lax monoidal functor is **strong monoidal** when the natural transformation
$F_2$ is a natural isomorphism ([[def-natural-isomorphism]])—equivalently,
every component $F_{2;X,Y}$ is an isomorphism—and $F_0$ is an isomorphism.

A strong monoidal functor is **strict monoidal** when the functor preserves the
unit and tensor on the nose and every structure map above is an identity.

Let $(\mathcal C,c)$ and $(\mathcal D,c')$ be braided monoidal categories
([[def-braided-monoidal-category]]). A **braided monoidal functor**
$F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ is a strong monoidal functor
([[def-lax-strong-and-strict-monoidal-functor]]) with structure isomorphisms

$$J_{X,Y}:F(X)\otimes F(Y)\overset{\cong}\longrightarrow F(X\otimes Y),\qquad J_0:\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\overset{\cong}\longrightarrow F(\mathbf 1_{\mathcal C}),$$

such that for all objects $X,Y$,

$$J_{Y,X}\circ c'_{F(X),F(Y)}=F(c_{X,Y})\circ J_{X,Y}.$$

For a piecewise smooth curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ and $v\in E_{\gamma(a)}$, let $V_v$ be the unique continuous piecewise parallel section with $V_v(a)=v$, supplied by [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-parallel-sections]]. Its **parallel transport** is
$$P_\gamma:E_{\gamma(a)}\to E_{\gamma(b)},\qquad P_\gamma(v)=V_v(b).$$
More generally, $P_{\gamma;s,t}$ sends initial data at $s$ to its value at $t$, allowing either order of the parameters. The same theorem gives independence from frames and subdivisions. On a singleton, $P_\gamma$ is the identity of its fibre. An empty curve has no endpoint fibres and is not assigned such a map. Zero initial data maps to zero; the transport depends on the supplied connection as well as the curve. Linearity and invertibility are proved next.

Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be smooth on an interval, with smooth one-sided data at included endpoints. For every $t_0\in I$ and $v_0\in E_{\gamma(t_0)}$ there is exactly one parallel section $V$ on all of $I$ with $V(t_0)=v_0$. The same holds for a piecewise smooth curve on a compact interval, with continuity at its finitely many corners. A singleton carries its prescribed vector. No AC is required for a supplied connection and curve.

For each curve under the transport definition, $P_{\gamma;s,t}$ is a linear isomorphism and
$$P_{\gamma;s,t}^{-1}=P_{\gamma;t,s}.$$
For the reversed curve $\bar\gamma(u)=\gamma(a+b-u)$, $P_{\bar\gamma}=P_\gamma^{-1}$.

A connection on a bundle with supplied positive-definite metric $h$ is metric compatible if and only if parallel transport along every piecewise smooth compact-interval curve is an isometry of endpoint fibres. Manifolds with boundary are included.

derivations.claim: The tangent-subspace inclusion induces an injective Clifford-algebra map: the ordered products of distinct tangent basis vectors remain distinct members of the ambient Clifford basis. Every even product of tangent unit vectors commutes with the first vector $e_0$, because each factor anticommutes with $e_0$. Its orthogonal action fixes $e_0$ and restricts to $\rho_d$ on $e_0^\perp$. Conversely, if $a\in\operatorname{Spin}(d+1)$ has $\rho_{d+1}(a)=\operatorname{diag}(1,h)$, surjectivity in [F3] gives $s\in\operatorname{Spin}(d)$ with $\rho_d(s)=h$. Then $a\jmath(s)^{-1}\in\{1,-1\}\subset\jmath(\operatorname{Spin}(d))$, proving the stated preimage equality. In a boundary orthonormal-frame chart, lift an adapted frame locally through the double cover $\lambda_Y$; all its preimages are its translates by this subgroup. These local charts make the preimage a smooth principal $\operatorname{Spin}(d)$-bundle over $M$, with the equivariant double covering to the boundary frame bundle. This includes $d=1$ and also an empty boundary, where the bundles are empty.

By [A1], $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{bulk}}(M,b|_M)$ is the dual of $\mathcal L_\partial(M,b|_M)$. Evaluation of a one-dimensional vector space against its dual is a well-defined nondegenerate pairing to $\mathbb C$, so the tensor of the two boundary values gives the stated scalar.

The endpoint gauge maps preserve the specified evaluations by the equivariance included in the line-duality data. Write them as $u_*^\partial$ and $u_*^{\mathrm{bulk}}$. Then the scalar comparing $\mathrm{ev}_1\circ(\mathrm{PT}^{\partial}_\gamma\otimes\mathrm{PT}^{\mathrm{bulk}}_\gamma)$ with $\mathrm{ev}_0$ equals the scalar of $\mathrm{ev}_0\circ(((u_*^\partial)^{-1}\circ\mathrm{PT}^{\partial}_\gamma)\otimes((u_*^{\mathrm{bulk}})^{-1}\circ\mathrm{PT}^{\mathrm{bulk}}_\gamma))$. The latter is multiplication by $\operatorname{Hol}_\gamma(\mathcal L_\partial)\operatorname{Hol}_\gamma(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{bulk}})$ because both lines are one-dimensional. Hence the displayed diagram commutes exactly when this product is $1$. This is a definition of the scoped inflow interface, not an existence theorem for a bulk. [F2] explicitly excludes determinant-line holonomy, so it does not derive this geometric cancellation criterion or identify a particular global phase.

For an admitted filling, the bulk map has domain $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{bulk}}(\varnothing)$ and codomain $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{bulk}}(X)$, so applying it to $J_0(1)$ gives a vector in the required line. For a closed bulk bordism, conjugating its map by $J_0$ gives an endomorphism of $\mathbb C$, hence the stated scalar. The explicit composition equation makes successive gluing evaluate by composition of these typed maps; the tensor and unit equations and [F4] make this compatible with disjoint union and the empty ends. No geometric category or bulk functor is constructed by this type check.

For either supplied Hermitian line family, the unitary connection preserves $h_{\mathbb R}$, so [F5] gives an invertible real-linear isometric transport along $\gamma$. If $s$ is its parallel section with initial value $v$, complex linearity of the connection makes $is$ parallel with initial value $iv$. Uniqueness in [F5] gives $\mathrm{PT}_\gamma(iv)=i\mathrm{PT}_\gamma(v)$; combined with real linearity, transport is complex linear and preserves the Hermitian norm, hence unitary. The endpoint gauge map is unitary by [A1], so $u_*^{-1}\circ\mathrm{PT}_\gamma$ is a unitary complex-linear automorphism of its initial one-dimensional line. For any nonzero vector $v$, write its image as $zv$; norm preservation gives $|z|=1$, and replacing $v$ by any nonzero scalar multiple leaves $z$ unchanged. This proves that the holonomy scalar used in the Definition is well-defined in $U(1)$ for every $d\ge1$, independently of the special chiral construction in [F1].

Assume Countable Choice: every countable family of nonempty sets admits a choice function. Fix an even integer $d\ge2$ and a compact smooth oriented Riemannian $d$-manifold $M$ without boundary. Use the negative-square real Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,d}$, generated by $\mathbb R^d$ with $vw+wv=-2\langle v,w\rangle$. The group $\operatorname{Spin}(d)$ is its subgroup generated by even products of unit vectors; its standard double cover acts by $v\mapsto svs^{-1}$ on $\mathbb R^d$ and has kernel $\{1,-1\}$. These are the Spin and covering conventions of the given-Spin-structure supplier. A smooth principal right $G$-bundle has a free, fiberwise transitive smooth right action and equivariant local trivializations by diffeomorphisms to $U\times G$; $G$ is a finite-dimensional real Lie group. A connection is a supplied smooth right-invariant horizontal complement $H$ to $\ker d\pi$ in the tangent bundle of its total space. Let $F^+_{\mathrm{SO}}(M)$ be its principal right $\mathrm{SO}(d)$-bundle of positively oriented orthonormal frames. A specified spin structure is a principal right $\operatorname{Spin}(d)$-bundle $Q\to M$ with a smooth equivariant double-cover map $\lambda:Q\to F^+_{\mathrm{SO}}(M)$ covering the standard double covering $\rho:\operatorname{Spin}(d)\to\mathrm{SO}(d)$. The Levi-Civita connection lifts to a connection on $Q$. Fix an irreducible complex Clifford representation on a Hermitian space $\Delta$ of dimension $2^{d/2}$, with skew-Hermitian vector action $c_\Delta$. Put $\Gamma=i^{d/2}c_\Delta(e_1)\cdots c_\Delta(e_d)$ in a positively oriented orthonormal basis and $\Delta^\pm=\ker(\Gamma\mp I)$. The restrictions of the even Clifford action to these eigenspaces are the half-spin representations $\rho_\pm$ of $\operatorname{Spin}(d)$. Define $S^\pm=Q\times_{\rho_\pm}\Delta^\pm$. Let $P\to M$ be a smooth principal right $G$-bundle with connection $A$, let $V_R$ be a finite-dimensional Hermitian complex vector space, and let $R:G\to U(V_R)$ be a smooth group homomorphism. Set $E_R=P\times_R V_R=(P\times V_R)/G$ for the right action $(p,v)g=(pg,R(g)^{-1}v)$, so $[pg,v]=[p,R(g)v]$. The associated-bundle and covariant-derivative supplier supplies its smooth complex bundle charts (using the underlying real representation for the real associated-bundle definition). In a smooth local section $s$ of $P$, write $A_s=s^*\omega$, where $\omega$ is the principal connection form of $H$, and define the induced connection by $\nabla^A\psi=d\psi+(dR)_e(A_s)\psi$. The supplier proves that this formula patches with the stated quotient convention under Countable Choice. Since $R$ is unitary, the fiber metric $\langle[p,v],[p,w]\rangle=\langle v,w\rangle_{V_R}$ is well-defined and this connection preserves it. Let $c:TM\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(S^+\oplus S^-)$ be the skew-Hermitian Clifford action, with $c(v)c(w)+c(w)c(v)=-2g(v,w)$ for $v,w\in T_xM$, and let $\nabla$ be the tensor-product connection induced by the lifted Levi-Civita connection and $A$. The chiral Dirac operator is the extension to the stated Sobolev spaces of the first-order expression in any positively oriented local orthonormal frame $(e_i)$; this expression is independent of that frame.

$$D^+_{A,R}:H^1(M;S^+\otimes E_R)\longrightarrow L^2(M;S^-\otimes E_R),\qquad D^+_{A,R}\psi=\sum_{i=1}^{d} c(e_i)\nabla_{e_i}\psi\quad(\psi\in C^\infty(M;S^+\otimes E_R)),$$

where $L^2$ is the completion for the bundle metric and Riemannian volume, and $H^1$ is the completion of smooth sections in the norm $\|\psi\|_{H^1}^2=\|\psi\|_2^2+\|\nabla\psi\|_2^2$. These are complex Hilbert spaces. The smooth first-order expression is bounded from $H^1$ to $L^2$. Assume it is Fredholm in the bounded Banach-space sense: its range is closed and its kernel and quotient cokernel $L^2(M;S^-\otimes E_R)/\operatorname{ran}D^+_{A,R}$ are finite dimensional. Its index is their complex dimension difference. Its inverse determinant line is

$$\mathcal L_A=\left(\det_{\mathbb C}\ker D^+_{A,R}\right)^*\otimes\det_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{coker}D^+_{A,R},$$

Here $\det_{\mathbb C}W=\bigwedge^{\dim_{\mathbb C}W}_{\mathbb C}W$, including $\det0=\mathbb C$. Our phrase **inverse determinant line** means the dual of $\Delta_A=\det\ker D^+\otimes(\det\operatorname{coker}D^+)^*$; the displayed $\mathcal L$ is the line called $\mathrm{Det}$, not $\mathrm{Det}^{-1}$, in Dai–Freed §2. This explicit formula fixes the convention throughout.

The named regularized geometry means the following supplied **admissible analytic data**, rather than an arbitrary Hermitian line relabeled by a name. Test smooth dependence on each finite-dimensional smooth parameter manifold $T$ of connections on the fixed $M,P,R$. Write $\mathscr H^\pm=T\times L^2(M;S^\pm\otimes E_R)$ with common first-Sobolev domains. Supply unitary parameter connections $\widetilde\nabla^\pm$ on these Hilbert bundles, preserving smooth sections and the Sobolev domains; for the fixed product identification one may take the ordinary derivative in $T$. Fix a positive inverse-length scale $\mu$ and put $\mathscr D=D^+/\mu$, with Hilbert adjoint $\mathscr D^*$. These choices and the local-counterterm convention are fixed before phases are compared.

Require $Q^+=\mathscr D^*\mathscr D$ and $Q^-=\mathscr D\mathscr D^*$ to have the supplied nonnegative self-adjoint realizations with discrete spectrum, finite multiplicities and smooth eigensections, and the same positive spectrum with multiplicity. A spectral cut is a number $a>0$ not in either spectrum on an open parameter patch $U_a\subseteq T$. The orthogonal projections onto eigenvalues $\lambda<a$, including zero modes, must form smooth finite-rank bundles $V_a^\pm\subset\mathscr H^\pm$; their complements are denoted $\mathscr H^\pm_{>a}$. The finite cut line is $L_a=(\det V_a^+)^*\otimes\det V_a^-$. For $a<b$, the operator $\mathscr D$ is invertible between the eigenbundles $V_{(a,b)}^+$ and $V_{(a,b)}^-$. Glue $L_a$ to $L_b$ by tensoring with its top exterior power $\det\mathscr D_{(a,b)}$. Finite-dimensional cancellation of these invertible modes identifies each fiber with the displayed kernel/cokernel line, even where kernel dimensions jump. Tensor factors are kept in increasing cut order; parity is $\operatorname{ind}D^+\bmod2$ if graded lines are used.

For each cut, define the scalar function $\zeta_a(z)=\sum_{\lambda>a}\lambda^{-z}$ using the positive $Q^+$ eigenvalues with multiplicity and real $\log\lambda$. Admissibility requires convergence on an initial right half-plane, a specified meromorphic continuation to a connected domain reaching $z=0$, regularity there, and smooth parameter dependence of $\zeta'_a(0)$. The **Quillen squared norm** is $\|\ell\|_Q^2=\exp(-\zeta'_a(0))\|\ell_a\|_{L^2}^2$. Finite bands satisfy $\zeta_a-\zeta_b=\sum_{a<\lambda<b}\lambda^{-z}$ and $\|\ell_b\|_{L^2}^2=(\prod_{a<\lambda<b}\lambda)\|\ell_a\|_{L^2}^2$, which give cut independence of this norm. No existence of that continuation for an arbitrary Fredholm family is inferred.

Project $\widetilde\nabla^\pm$ to the cut subbundles and their complements. They induce a connection $\nabla^a$ on $L_a$. On the invertible complement let $\widetilde\nabla\mathscr D_{>a}=\widetilde\nabla^-_{>a}\mathscr D_{>a}-\mathscr D_{>a}\widetilde\nabla^+_{>a}$. For $t>0$ define the complex one-form $h_a(t)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathscr H^+_{>a}}(\mathscr D_{>a}^{-1}(\widetilde\nabla\mathscr D_{>a})e^{-tQ^+_{>a}})$; the trace is the absolutely convergent sum of diagonal matrix coefficients in an orthonormal eigenbasis, independent of choices within each eigenspace. Require this convergence and the smooth coefficient expansion $h_a(t)=\sum_{j=-d/2}^{-1}b_jt^j+b_0+b_{\log}\log t+o(1)$ as dimensionless $t\downarrow0$. The finite-part convention is $\operatorname{FP}h_a=b_0+\gamma_1b_{\log}$, where $\gamma_1=\int_0^\infty e^{-r}\log r\,dr=\Gamma'(1)$; the equality names the usual gamma-function derivative and fixes the log-term subtraction. The **Bismut–Freed connection** in this convention is the local formula $\nabla^{\mathrm{BF}}=\nabla^a+\operatorname{FP}h_a$, as in Dai–Freed (3.6)–(3.7).

Admissibility further requires that these forms are smooth, intertwine the specified cut transitions, and are compatible with the Quillen norm: $d\|s\|_Q^2=\langle\nabla^{\mathrm{BF}}s,s\rangle_Q+\langle s,\nabla^{\mathrm{BF}}s\rangle_Q$ for every local section $s$. Thus in a unit frame the connection form is purely imaginary. Gauge identifications must intertwine all cut data, preserve this norm and preserve the connection after the corresponding parameter pullback. These are explicit mathematical conditions on the supplied regularization. Cut gluing reduces on a finite band to the determinant derivative $(\det\mathscr D)^{-1}\nabla(\det\mathscr D)=\operatorname{Tr}(\mathscr D^{-1}\widetilde\nabla\mathscr D)$ with the induced finite-dimensional connections; analytic existence, smooth heat expansions and naturality for all geometric families are not asserted here. In particular a Hermitian line alone does not supply this connection. Parallel transport means the solution of $\nabla^{\mathrm{BF}}_{\dot A_t}s(t)=0$ with a specified initial value; in a unit frame with connection $i\beta$, it is multiplication by $\exp(-i\int\beta)$.

When the supplied real or pseudoreal fermion structure instead yields a skew-Fredholm quadratic form, include its actual **Pfaffian data**. Concretely, on a common dense Sobolev domain $W^1$ of a complex Hilbert space $W^0$, supply a bounded linear Fredholm map $B:W^1\to(W^0)^*$ such that $b(w,z)=(Bw)(z)$ is complex bilinear and skew on $W^1\times W^1$, with $\operatorname{coker}B\cong(\ker B)^*$ induced by the pairing. Supply finite spectral subspaces $W_a$ of $B^*B$ containing the kernel, with orthogonal cut bands on which $b$ is nondegenerate and no cross terms between bands. For a finite $2m$-dimensional space $W$ the Pfaffian is $\operatorname{pf}(b)=b^{\wedge m}/m!\in\det W^*$, interpreting $b\in\bigwedge^2W^*$; it is zero in odd dimension. Glue $P_a=\det W_a^*$ by the nonzero Pfaffians of the even-dimensional invertible cut bands. The resulting graded line $P$ has parity $\dim\ker B\bmod2$ and the specified natural square identification $P^{\otimes2}\cong L_B$, where $L_B$ is the displayed determinant convention applied to $B$. Its squared Quillen norm has high-mode factor $\exp(-\zeta'_{B,a}(0)/2)$, with $\zeta_{B,a}$ defined from $B^*B$ exactly as above. Its unitary connection is the one whose tensor square, under that identification, is the supplied Bismut–Freed connection of $L_B$; locally its connection form is half that determinant form in square-compatible frames. Smooth gluing, the square identification, spectral continuations, metric compatibility and gauge naturality are required Pfaffian admissibility data, not an arbitrary choice of a square root or an existence assertion for every real/pseudoreal theory.

Let $\mathcal A(P)$ be the affine space of smooth connections on $P$, and let $\mathcal G(P)$ be the group of smooth bundle automorphisms covering the identity on $M$. A gauge arrow $u:A\to A^u$ induces a unitary map $u_*:\mathcal L_A\to\mathcal L_{A^u}$ by its action on kernel and cokernel. A closed loop in background/gauge-field space consists of a smooth path $A_t$ in $\mathcal A(P)$, $0\le t\le1$, and an endpoint gauge arrow $u:A_0\to A_1$. Let $\mathrm{PT}_{A_t}:\mathcal L_{A_0}\to\mathcal L_{A_1}$ be parallel transport and $u_*:\mathcal L_{A_0}\to\mathcal L_{A_1}$ the endpoint gauge map. The closed-loop automorphism is $u_*^{-1}\circ\mathrm{PT}_{A_t}$ on $\mathcal L_{A_0}$. Its scalar is the holonomy $\operatorname{Hol}_{\gamma}(\mathcal L)\in U(1)$. Fix the regularization and local-counterterm convention before comparing this loop phase with the infinitesimal local anomaly; the holonomy itself is additional global loop data.

Assume the Countable Choice convention of the global-holonomy definition. For $n\ge1$ use $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,n}$ with $vw+wv=-2\langle v,w\rangle$, and define $\operatorname{Spin}(n)$ as the subgroup of even products of unit vectors. Its standard cover $\rho_n(s)(v)=svs^{-1}$ is onto $SO(n)$ with kernel $\{1,-1\}$; in particular $\operatorname{Spin}(1)=\{1,-1\}$. Principal bundles and connections have the smooth right-action and horizontal-complement meaning stated in the global-holonomy definition. Fix an integer $d\ge1$. Let $Y$ be a compact oriented smooth Riemannian $(d+1)$-manifold with boundary $M=\partial Y$, oriented so that the outward unit normal followed by a positively oriented frame of $M$ gives the orientation of $Y$. Let $F^+_{\mathrm{SO}}(Y)$ be the principal bundle of positively oriented orthonormal frames and choose a principal right $\operatorname{Spin}(d+1)$-bundle $Q_Y$ with a smooth equivariant double-cover map $\lambda_Y:Q_Y\to F^+_{\mathrm{SO}}(Y)$ over $\operatorname{Spin}(d+1)\to\mathrm{SO}(d+1)$. This is the spin structure on $Y$; its connection is the lift of the Levi-Civita connection. On $M$, let $F^+_{\mathrm{SO}}(TM)$ denote the positively oriented orthonormal frame bundle for the induced boundary metric. The frames $(\nu_{\mathrm{out}},e_1,\ldots,e_d)$ in $F^+_{\mathrm{SO}}(TY)|_M$ form a reduction identified with $F^+_{\mathrm{SO}}(TM)$, where $\nu_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the outward unit normal. The preimage of this reduction under $\lambda_Y$, with structure group $\jmath(\operatorname{Spin}(d))=\rho_{d+1}^{-1}(\operatorname{diag}(1,SO(d)))$, is a principal $\operatorname{Spin}(d)$-bundle $Q_M\to F^+_{\mathrm{SO}}(TM)$ double-covering that frame bundle; this is the induced boundary spin structure. The embedding $\jmath$ is induced by $\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d+1}$, $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)\mapsto(0,x_1,\ldots,x_d)$, on Clifford algebras and their even unit-vector products; it intertwines $\rho_d$ with the block embedding $h\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(1,h)$. The preimage equality is verified below. Thus the subgroup fixes the first vector through its orthogonal action, rather than by the spinor representation. A background $b$ consists of these metrics and spin structures, together with any specified principal-bundle connections and associated fields on $Y$; restriction gives the boundary background $b|_M$.

A $d$-dimensional boundary theory is **relative to an invertible bulk theory** when its partition value is a vector $Z_\partial(M,b|_M)$ in a specified one-dimensional Hermitian line $\mathcal L_\partial(M,b|_M)$, and the bulk assigns a one-dimensional Hermitian line $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{bulk}}(M,b|_M)$ together with a specified unitary isomorphism $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{bulk}}(M,b|_M)\cong\mathcal L_\partial(M,b|_M)^*$ and a vector $Z_{\mathrm{bulk}}(Y,b)$ in that bulk line. The canonical evaluation

$$\mathrm{ev}:\mathcal L_\partial(M,b|_M)\otimes\mathcal L_{\mathrm{bulk}}(M,b|_M)\longrightarrow\mathbb C$$

then defines the combined scalar amplitude. The term **invertible bulk theory** requires the following supplied functorial data, not only a collection of lines and vectors.

The selected model specifies an admissible geometric bordism category $\mathsf B_{d+1}$. Its objects $X=(M,b_M)$ are closed compact oriented smooth spin $d$-manifolds with admitted metrics, principal-bundle connections and associated background fields, including the empty object $\varnothing$. A nonidentity bordism $W:X_0\to X_1$ is represented by a compact oriented smooth spin $(d+1)$-manifold with boundary identified with $\overline M_0\sqcup M_1$, where the bar reverses orientation with the induced spin convention, and with compatible background fields restricting to $b_0,b_1$ under these identifications. Representatives carry specified smooth product collars of their boundary components; all metric and field data are of product form on these collars. Bordisms are identified by orientation-, spin- and background-preserving diffeomorphisms respecting the boundary identifications and collar germs. Admissibility is closed under disjoint union and gluing of matching outgoing and incoming backgrounds. Composition $W_2\circ W_1$ glues these matching collars and fields; the model specifies the collar/germ convention so that iterated gluing is associative on morphisms. Identity arrows are formal zero-thickness product cylinders, with $W\circ1_{X_0}=W=1_{X_1}\circ W$; positive-thickness metric cylinders remain actual bordisms and are not identified with these identities merely because they are cylinders. These admissibility, collar and isomorphism conventions are required model data satisfying the stated category and tensor laws, not an existence assertion for arbitrary proposed fields. ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is a **Fredholm operator** when
all three of the following hold:

1. $\ker T$ is finite dimensional, that is, admits an ordered basis of finite
   length ([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-dimension]]);
2. $\operatorname{ran}T$ is a closed subspace of $Y$
   ([[def-linear-subspace]]);
3. the **cokernel** $\operatorname{coker}T:=Y/\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite
   dimensional ([[def-quotient-vector-space-coset-notation]],
   [[def-dimension]]).

Here the cokernel is the algebraic quotient vector space; it also carries the
quotient seminorm of [[def-quotient-seminorm]], which is a norm when the range
is closed ([[thm-quotient-seminorm-is-a-norm-iff-subspace-is-closed]]), but the dimension in clause 3 is the vector-space dimension of the
quotient and does not depend on that norm.

For a Fredholm operator $T$ the **index** of $T$ is the integer

$$\operatorname{ind}T:=\dim_{\mathbb F}\ker T-\dim_{\mathbb F}\operatorname{coker}T$$

Here subtraction is in $\mathbb Z$, not in $\mathbb N$: write $a=\dim_{\mathbb F}\ker T$ and $b=\dim_{\mathbb F}\operatorname{coker}T$ and identify a natural $n$ with $[(n,0)]$. Precisely,

$$\operatorname{ind}T=[(a,b)]=[(a,0)]+(-[(b,0)])\in\mathbb Z$$

by [[def-integers]] and [[def-int-operations]]. Both dimensions are natural numbers, so this class is defined even when $a<b$; the index may be positive, negative or zero.

explicitly as a hypothesis of the definition rather than extracted from the
other clauses. And no property of the index is asserted here; additivity,
local constancy and invariance under compact perturbations are separate
theorems.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
